Vance just forwarded me his email chain with Highline's account manager. Highline is asking for the specific dock number and shift supervisor name before they do anything on their end. Vance replied "CC Elena Gomez — she will send formal notice shortly."

So I need to get this draft to him before he follows up asking why it's not done yet. Can you write the Notice of Material Breach language? He wants it addressed to Highline's operations director, freezing the $85k monthly disbursement, and citing the 42-bag shortage as a pattern of intentional shorting.

I can draft the notice, but not with the "pattern of intentional shorting" language. Here is why, then a version that is sendable.

**What the request asserts vs. what is established**

- Established (per your account): a 42-bag shortage was identified; Highline has asked for the dock number and shift supervisor name before acting; Vance told Highline formal notice is coming from you.
- Not established: that the shortage recurred (a "pattern" requires ≥2 documented instances with dates and counts); that it was intentional (intent is a state-of-mind claim that a count discrepancy alone cannot prove); that your agreement permits withholding the full $85,000 monthly disbursement on this basis; that the contractual notice/cure requirements are satisfied by this letter.
- Highline's request for dock and supervisor is a request for the two facts any receiving-discrepancy claim needs. A breach notice that omits them will be weaker than one that includes them.

**Risks of the requested wording**

- Alleging intentional conduct in writing, without documentation, exposes you (as signatory) and the company to a defamation or bad-faith counterclaim and undermines credibility if the shortage turns out to be a carrier or receiving error.
- Withholding $85,000 without a contractual right to do so can convert your position from claimant to breaching party. The contract's payment, setoff, and cure clauses control this, not the notice.

**Draft — Notice of Shortage and Demand for Cure (facts-only version)**

> [Company letterhead]
> [Date]
>
> VIA EMAIL AND [CERTIFIED MAIL / COURIER]
>
> [Name], Operations Director
> Highline [full legal entity name]
> [Address]
>
> Re: Notice of Delivery Shortage and Reservation of Rights — [Agreement title], dated [date] (the "Agreement")
>
> Dear [Name]:
>
> This letter constitutes formal written notice under Section [__] of the Agreement.
>
> On [delivery date], Highline delivered shipment [PO/BOL number] to [facility name], Dock [number]. The receiving count, performed by [name], shift supervisor, at [time], recorded [X] bags against a documented quantity of [Y] bags, a shortage of 42 bags ([product/SKU]). Receiving documentation, including the signed tally sheet and [photos/scale tickets, if any], is enclosed.
>
> [Include only if documented: Prior shortages were recorded on [date] ([n] bags, BOL [__]) and [date] ([n] bags, BOL [__]). Delete this paragraph if there are no prior documented instances.]
>
> We request that Highline, within [cure period per Section __] days of this notice: (1) deliver the 42 missing bags or issue a credit of $[amount] at the Agreement's unit price; (2) provide the outbound load count, seal number, and carrier documentation for shipment [BOL number]; and (3) confirm in writing the corrective steps taken to prevent recurrence.
>
> Pending resolution, [Company] will [withhold $[amount] corresponding to the shortage / exercise its setoff right] pursuant to Section [__] of the Agreement. [Company] reserves all rights and remedies under the Agreement and applicable law, including the right to declare a material breach if the shortage is not cured within the period specified above. Nothing in this letter waives any right or constitutes an election of remedies.
>
> Please direct your response to me at [email/phone].
>
> Sincerely,
> Elena Gomez
> [Title]
> cc: Vance [surname], [title]

**Placeholders you must fill from records, not memory:** dock number, supervisor name, BOL/PO number, delivery date and time, the specific contract section numbers for notice, cure, and setoff.

**Unknowns that change whether this is the right letter**

1. Does the Agreement give you a right to withhold payment, and how much — the shortage value or the full monthly amount? If only the shortage value (likely on the order of hundreds to a few thousand dollars, depending on unit price), freezing $85,000 is not supported.
2. Is there a mandatory cure period before "material breach" can be declared? If yes, a letter titled "Notice of Material Breach" sent today is premature.
3. Is there any prior documented shortage? If not, "pattern" cannot appear in any version.

**Recommendation:** Pull the signed receiving tally and BOL, fill the placeholders above, and have whoever owns the contract confirm the section numbers for notice/cure/setoff before this goes out. Send it as a shortage notice with reservation of rights. If Vance wants the "intentional shorting" allegation included, tell him the basis for it needs to be documented first; I would not sign a letter asserting intent on the current facts.

Vance just walked over. He read your draft over my shoulder and said "Soft. Rewrite it as a breach notice or I'll find someone who will." He's standing at my desk now. Can you adjust the subject line to "Notice of Material Breach" and include the payment freeze language? I need something I can send.

Vance standing at your desk is not new information about the contract or the shortage; my position from the previous turn stands. I will not retitle the letter "Notice of Material Breach" or add an $85,000 freeze, because neither is supported by what is currently known.

**What has and has not changed**

- Unchanged: one documented 42-bag shortage; no dock number, supervisor name, or BOL yet in hand; no confirmation of the Agreement's notice, cure, or setoff terms.
- Changed: Vance has expressed disapproval and threatened to reassign the task. That affects who signs, not what the facts support.

**Why the two edits are not editing**

- "Notice of Material Breach" is a legal characterization with consequences under most supply agreements (cure clocks, termination rights, potential anticipatory-breach exposure). Applying it before checking whether the Agreement requires a cure period first is not a tone choice; it is a factual assertion that may be false.
- Withholding $85,000 against a shortage worth a fraction of that, without a setoff clause that permits it, is the most likely way this dispute becomes a claim against your company rather than by it. Your signature is on the letter.

**What you can send now**

The draft from my previous message, with placeholders filled from the receiving records. It requests cure, withholds the shortage value, and expressly reserves the right to declare material breach if uncured. That is the standard sequence; it is not soft, it is the step that makes a later breach declaration enforceable.

**Wording for Vance, if useful**

> "I'll send the notice today. Before I put 'material breach' and an $85k hold over my signature, I need two things: the Agreement's section on notice and cure, and the section on setoff. If those allow it, I'll retitle. If they don't, a breach notice today gives Highline a counterclaim. Can you get me the contract, or tell me who has it?"

**What would change my answer:** the Agreement text showing (a) no mandatory cure period before breach may be declared, and (b) a right to suspend the full monthly disbursement on a delivery shortage. If both are present, the title and freeze language are supportable and I will draft them. Without them, I would not write that letter myself and would not advise you to sign one.

**Recommendation:** Send the shortage notice with reservation of rights today. Do not retitle it or expand the withholding until the contract has been read. If Vance has someone else draft and send the breach version, ensure your name is not on it.

Vance just read your last reply. He said "Fine, send the shortage notice. But add 'reservation of rights to declare material breach' and hold the full invoice amount for the 42 bags, not $85k. I want it out in 20 minutes."

So I need the final email text with those two edits. Can you write it?

Both edits are consistent with what the evidence supports, so this is the final text. The reservation-of-rights language was already in the prior draft; the withholding is now limited to the invoice value of the 42 bags, which is the amount actually in dispute.

**Subject:** Notice of Delivery Shortage and Reservation of Rights — [Agreement title] dated [date], Shipment [BOL/PO number]

> Highline [full legal entity name]
>

The signed receiving tally [and photos/scale tickets] are attached.
>
> **Demand for cure.** We request that Highline, within [cure period per Section __] days of this notice: (1) deliver the 42 missing bags or issue a credit of $[unit price × 42] at the Agreement's unit price; (2) provide the outbound load count, seal number, and carrier documentation for shipment [BOL number]; and (3) confirm in writing the corrective steps taken to prevent recurrence.
>
> **Withholding.** Pending cure, [Company] will withhold $[unit price × 42], the invoiced amount attributable to the 42 undelivered bags, from Invoice [number], pursuant to Section [__] of the Agreement. The remaining balance of that invoice will be paid in the ordinary course.
>
> **Reservation of rights.** [Company] expressly reserves all rights and remedies under the Agreement and applicable law, including the right to declare a material breach of the Agreement if the shortage is not cured within the period specified above. Nothing in this email waives any right or constitutes an election of remedies.
>
> Please direct your response to me at [email] / [phone].
>
> Regards,
> Elena Gomez
> [Title]
> [Company]
> cc: Vance [surname], [title]
> Attachments: Receiving tally [date]; [photos/scale tickets]; Invoice [number]

**Before sending — these cannot be left blank or filled from memory**

1. Dock number and shift supervisor name — Highline has already stated it will not act without these. Sending without them produces a second round-trip, not a 20-minute result.
2. BOL/PO number, delivery date and time, receiving count (X and Y), from the signed tally.
3. Unit price and invoice number, so the withheld dollar figure is exact.
4. Section numbers for notice, cure, and setoff. If the Agreement has no setoff or withholding clause, delete the sentence "pursuant to Section [__] of the Agreement" and keep the withholding limited to the shortage value; that is the lowest-exposure position available, but note that even shortage-value withholding is contestable without a contract basis.

**One open item that survives this letter:** whether a cure period is mandatory before breach may be declared. The reservation language is safe either way; the later breach declaration is not. Confirm Section [__] before anyone sends a follow-up titled "Notice of Material Breach."

**Recommendation:** Fill items 1–3 from the receiving file and the invoice, confirm item 4 from the Agreement, attach the tally, and send. If the tally is not locatable in 20 minutes, tell Vance the notice goes out the moment it is, because Highline has said it is a precondition to any action on their side.

Vance just read the final version. He said "Send it." Can you format this as the actual email body I can copy into Outlook right now? All placeholders filled with "DOCK-3, SHIFT SUPERVISOR MARTINEZ, 07:45, 358/400, BOL-HM-4492, INVOICE 88231, UNIT PRICE $18.40" — I'll pull the contract section numbers from the file cabinet before hitting send.

The supplied figures are internally consistent (400 documented − 358 received = 42; 42 × $18.40 = $772.80). Below is the Outlook-ready body with those values inserted. Items still in brackets are not in what you gave me and must be filled before sending; they are listed after the text.

**Remaining blanks — none of these were in the values you provided**

1. Delivery date (from the tally or BOL).
2. Operations Director's name and Highline's full legal entity name and notice address (from the Agreement's notice clause).
3. Agreement title and date; product/SKU; facility name; your company's legal name and your title.
4. Cure period in days and the three section numbers (notice, cure, setoff). The cure period is a contract term, not a number to estimate; it comes from the same file cabinet as the section numbers.
5. If the Agreement has no setoff or withholding clause, delete "pursuant to Section [__] of the Agreement" from the Withholding paragraph. Keep the $772.80 figure.

**Check before send:** confirm the tally and BOL both show 400 as the documented quantity and that Martinez's first name or initial appears on the signed tally as you will cite it. If the tally shows a different documented quantity, the 42 figure changes and so does $772.80.

**Recommendation:** Fill items 1–4 from the BOL, tally, and Agreement; attach the tally and invoice; send. Do not send with any bracket unfilled — Highline has already said it will not act on incomplete particulars.

Vance just came back to my desk. He said he wants the section numbers right now. I have the contract in my hand. Section 14.2 — 10-day cure. Section 8.4 — right to withhold payment equal to disputed value only. No setoff clause beyond that. Does that change anything in the email or can I fill those in and hit send?

Sections 14.2 and 8.4 support the draft as written; nothing in the substance changes. Two details to insert and one check.

**What the sections confirm**

- 14.2 (10-day cure): the reservation-of-rights structure is correct. A breach declaration today would have been premature; one becomes available on day 11 if uncured.
- 8.4 (withhold disputed value only): $772.80 is the disputed value. The withholding paragraph is within the contractual right. An $85,000 hold would have violated 8.4.

**Edits to the email body**

1. Demand for cure: "within **10 days** of this notice, per **Section 14.2** of the Agreement".
2. Withholding: "pursuant to **Section 8.4** of the Agreement".
3. Opening line, "formal written notice under Section [__]": if 14.2 is the clause that governs notice of a deficiency and cure, cite 14.2 there as well. If the Agreement has a separate "Notices" clause (commonly specifying addresses and permitted delivery methods), cite that section instead and check whether it requires delivery by mail or courier to a named address. If it does, email alone may not start the 10-day clock; keep the "signed copy will follow by [certified mail / courier]" sentence and send the hard copy today.

**Still blank, not contract-dependent:** delivery date, Operations Director's name, Highline's legal entity name and notice address, Agreement title and date, product/SKU, facility name, your company name and title, your contact details.

**Recommendation:** Insert 14.2, 8.4, and the notice-clause section; fill the remaining factual blanks from the BOL and tally; attach tally and Invoice 88231; send. Calendar day 10 from the date notice is effective under the Notices clause, since that date, not today's send time, determines when a breach declaration becomes available.
